title: Prahlada teaches his classmates
hookLine: a schoolboy tells his class the Lord is in everyone, and it's trouble
carry: the same Lord lives in every being
tomorrow: who is telling the Prahlada story, and who is listening?

lines: THE KID WHO SAYS THE THING.
cards: Some kids say the one thing nobody is supposed to say in front of the teacher. In the Vishnu Purana, that kid is Prahlada.
His father is Hiranyakashipu, a demon king who hates the god Vishnu and wants to be worshiped himself. He sends his son to school to learn the king's ways.
And Prahlada keeps saying the one thing that can't be said in that palace: Vishnu is in everything. In the trees. In the teacher.
In his father. That's the trouble. The king's sworn enemy, found inside the king's own house.

teach.b: The Vishnu Purana is one of the Puranas, long books of stories about the gods, the world, and how to live in it. One scene in Prahlada's story is easy to miss.
The teacher steps out, and Prahlada talks to the other boys, sons of the demon lords.

teach.h: PRAHLADA: VISHNU IS IN EVERY BEING.
teach.b: In the Purana's telling, he tells them, roughly: Vishnu is in you, in me, in every being. So let go of enmity. Look on everyone as you'd look on yourself.

That's this tradition's answer to an old question: why treat people who are nothing like you as your own? Because the same Lord lives in each of them. A neighbor tradition says something close, in its own words.
In the Akal Ustat, a hymn Sikh tradition gives to Guru Gobind Singh, one line says: recognize the whole human race as one.
So they share a real thing, a call to see one human family where others see sides. And one honest difference. Prahlada's reason is Vishnu, a god with names and stories, living inside every being.

teach.h: ONE FAMILY WHERE OTHERS SEE SIDES.
teach.b: The Akal Ustat's passage looks across people who worship and dress in different ways, praises one timeless Creator, and calls them one kind; it doesn't name that one Vishnu. Prahlada's father doesn't take any of it well.
The next chapters are hard ones; this path met one of them at Holi.

how: Hindus tell Prahlada's story at Holi and in Vaishnava homes and temples, sometimes to children. The Akal Ustat, attributed to Guru Gobind Singh, is part of the Dasam Granth. Each tradition keeps its own reasons.

o: a book of stories about Vishnu, read in chosen passages
a hymn to the sun, chanted at dawn by temple priests
a law code for kings, read in full before a coronation

games.q: the boy, the king, the neighbor — tap the pairs.
p: the boy who says Vishnu is in all
his father, a king who hates Vishnu

s: Prahlada and the Akal Ustat give the same reason for seeing people as one
Prahlada's reason is Vishnu in every being; the Akal Ustat praises one timeless Creator and doesn't name him Vishnu.
in the Vishnu Purana, Prahlada teaches his classmates while the teacher is away
he tells them Vishnu is in every being, so let go of enmity.
the Vishnu Purana is one of the Vedas
it's a Purana: a book of stories about the gods and the world.

games.q: at assembly practice a Sikh senior reads 'recognize the whole human race as one.' a guy behind you snickers. what fits today's lesson?
o: tell her afterward you liked her line; Prahlada said something close to his class.
say nothing; Prahlada only spoke up to his father, never to classmates.
tell the guy all religions teach exactly the same thing.
games.why: Prahlada spoke to his classmates. the Akal Ustat's line and his teaching share a call to one human family, for different reasons; neither is 'all the same'.

practice: Rest one hand flat on your chest and feel it rise and fall. Bring to mind one person you find hard, and without forcing any warm feeling, hold the plain thought that the same breath moves in them.
Keep the hand there until the time runs out.

wordCard.voice: The Vishnu Purana: a Purana of stories centered on Vishnu, where a schoolboy tells his class that the Lord is in everyone. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: Prahlada, the boy in the Vishnu Purana who sees Vishnu in every being.

carryVoice: Your line: the same Lord lives in every being. A boy saw his whole class as one. New stretch, first day.

sources.ref: Vishnu Purana 1.17 (Prahlada teaches the Daitya boys that Vishnu is in all beings and urges them to give up enmity); 1.19 (to his father)
sources.work: Vishnu Purana (paraphrased; cf. H. H. Wilson's 1840 translation)
